prompt: A service reads a user's record under a `users` lock, and the record says which of 1,024 shard locks the request must also take. A colleague suggests preventing deadlock by acquiring all needed locks up front, all or nothing. Why is this a poor fit?

options.text: Acquiring locks all-or-nothing is impossible in Python
options.explanation: It is easy to build (for example, take a global 'acquisition' lock, then try-lock each one and back off if any fails). The issue is what you'd have to request.
Priority inversion is about a high-priority thread waiting on a low-priority holder. It is unrelated to how many locks are requested at once.

options.text: It doesn't break any Coffman condition
options.explanation: It does: a thread that waits holding nothing breaks hold and wait. The problem is cost, not correctness.

options.text: The required shard is not known initially; locking every possible shard would be conservative but expensive, so discovering and revalidating the set or imposing an order is preferable
options.explanation: The direct one-pass up-front scheme lacks its required lock set. It could over-lock, or use a separate discovery/revalidation protocol; this makes it a less natural fit than a known global order.

workedExample: The shard depends on protected state. A naive request-everything-before-reading scheme would take a large conservative set. Alternatives include reading the shard, releasing, acquiring the discovered set consistently and revalidating, or defining users before shard locks. Revalidation must itself respect that order; do not acquire users after shard if that reverses it.
